The three working files at indices 25–27 are unreviewed proposals and are not used as grants.

**A224, packet indices 0–1.** The whole grant has the balanced lattice fan, finite local support lemma, strict-growth obstruction, literal regularity failure, source conversion, and finite calibration. Its endpoint/reference parameters have actual finite PA domains; strictness uses positive active coefficients. For its fan, writing `S=A+B`, the raw origin mass is `4S²`, each of the two other masses is `B(4A+3B)`, total degree is `4A²+16AB+10B²`, and the contact defect is `-4(C-B) epsilon S²`. It does not classify arbitrary real-reference pairs or establish real regularization for every pair. Our main proof uses none of its obstruction calculations; we retain them to preserve the original scope.

**B225, indices 2–3.** All seven main geometric units are retained: saturated normal length, stationary density, finite-global noncompactness, positive spanning of a fan, a positive relation, continuous PC maximum propagation, and the chart-dependent consequences. Density is actual `weight × cell covolume`, and the primitive projection length is `cell covolume / facet covolume`. A positive finite globally embedded cycle in positive dimension is noncompact; this is not a theorem excluding every abstract compact atlas. The original compact rational-minimum argument needs its stated finite bounded compatible decomposition. Our L2 reconstructs the local flux proof and does not borrow an unqualified compact conclusion.

**R230, indices 4–5.** Whole units retained: uniform rational star geometry, positive spanning, two rational Jensen bounds, local bounds without an a priori boundedness premise, feasible-face density, continuous completion including irrational centers/shared faces, the fan criterion, the unrestricted actual envelope, compact-chart consequences, and a fixed density obstruction. The rational-point discontinuity diagnostic remains a distinct obstruction to the printed all-PC formulation.

**S262, indices 6–11.** All nineteen scoped results and their full proofs, argument file, ledger, material-change record, clarification and acceptance record are retained. Their coverage is finite support/circuit cones, strict affine floor, necessary flat relations at noncontact, exact bounded PA roof obstructions, the finite-PA contact characterization, rational-reference jet realization, raw degree/integration-by-parts identities, differences of relative PC test functions, positive-functional completion, the exact continuity scopes and contact stability, the coupled two-plane and non-PA endpoint calculations, the finite-global literal obstruction, and the entire graph sector. The all-continuous graph sector uses actual real coefficients, primitive/Stieltjes completion, and a contact criterion from its graph relation cone. It is not all-face higher-dimensional gluing. The retained counterexample to global weak/BL uniformity has diverging relative bounds. Historical failed source records stay failed.

**S272, indices 12–17.** All thirteen scoped results and all annotations are retained: finite raw calibration/IBP; the rational all-face coefficient cone; exact extraction of a positive rational component from an actual real reference; positive convex rational-reference decomposition; auxiliary DC and moment/height estimates; actual-reference operator completion and contact stability; separate exact flat-jet realization; strict-floor and PA roof witnesses; and the finite-PA obstruction criterion. The actual reference is never rounded: in its minimal active face the decomposition is exactly `gamma=gamma'+epsilon gamma0` with rational positive `gamma0`. The fixed-bound height estimate has the form `K_C=(2d/epsilon) C deg(gamma)+J0`. It is a bound in the genuine completed global domain. Real signed/zero weights, zero-mass zero operator, and the separate dimension-zero case are retained. No mixed operator is applied in this paper to the auxiliary non-PA `F` or to a lone unbalanced cell. **S291, indices 18–24.** All seventeen scoped results, the full argument/ledger/scope files, the source correction, reader clarification and whole-acceptance record are retained. # Status, domain, and the exact assertions

The inputs working296, working297, and working299 are proposals rather than grants. We verify them below without importing their proofs as accepted results. The six supplied whole grants are A224, B225, R230, S262, S272, and S291, with their supplied source and reader qualifications. They are used only at their stated scope. In particular, the main argument does not invoke a compact maximum principle on a noncompact space. It does not invoke an operator on a lone unbalanced cell, or on a non-piecewise-affine intermediate extension. The detailed source ledger is a separate artifact. Source quotations and source pixels have not been incorporated in this document.

Let $X$ be a finite pure $d$-dimensional rational polyhedral complex globally embedded in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space with a fixed lattice. All its closed faces are retained. Distinct cells meet in common faces. Fix a rational refinement of this complex. For every top cell $\sigma$, its lattice is the saturated lattice in $T_\sigma=\Span(\sigma-\sigma)$. The top weights $w_\sigma$ are strictly positive actual real numbers. At every codimension-one face $\rho$, balancing means
$$
\sum_{\sigma\succ\rho} w_\sigma u_{\sigma/\rho}=0
\quad\hbox{in the ambient quotient by }T_\rho,
$$
where $u_{\sigma/\rho}$ is the primitive quotient lattice vector directed into $\sigma$. Balancing is required at every such face, including every face which would otherwise be a boundary. No rationality of the weights is assumed.

A *printed PCC* is the following finite inequality. At a center $y$ in a face $\tau$, choose rational endpoints $x_i$ in assigned cells $\sigma_i\succeq\tau$ and nonnegative real coefficients $\alpha_i$ such that $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$ and $\sum_i\alpha_i x_i=y$. The center is allowed to be real; the printed definition does not require it to be rational. The inequality is
$$ f(y)\leq\sum_i\alpha_i f(x_i). $$
The printed-PC hypothesis means that these inequalities hold for the rational structures and incidences in the definition. We will use the fixed refinement, and L0 needs only its rational-center subfamily. Continuity of $f$ is a separate, indispensable hypothesis. We do not assume that an arbitrary function satisfying the printed rational-endpoint inequalities is continuous.

Let $\gamma$ be an actual continuous real piecewise-affine function affine on each cell of the fixed refinement. Put
$$
G=\max_\sigma\|a_\sigma\|,
\qquad \gamma|_\sigma(x)=\langle a_\sigma,x\rangle+b_\sigma,
\quad a_\sigma\in T_\sigma.
$$
Here $a_\sigma$ is the intrinsic gradient, orthogonally embedded in the ambient space. Faces inherit the same bound. Neither convexity nor printed-PC nor positive growth of $\gamma$ is needed in the main assertion.
We take $C\geq0$. If the complex is empty, all conclusions are vacuous and we set $G=A_X=B_X=0$; henceforth the main proof treats a nonempty complex.

**Theorem 1 (working299, all six units).** There are finite constants $A_X,B_X$ depending on the fixed cell geometry and its Euclidean metric, and not on $f$, its location, $C$, or the values of $\gamma$, with the following property. If $f$ is continuous and printed-PC and $|f-\gamma|\leq C$ on $X$, then every closed convex cell has global Euclidean Lipschitz constant at most $A_XC+B_XG$. At every $y\in X$ there is an ambient vector $p_y$ of norm at most the same bound such that
$$
f(x)\geq f(y)+\langle p_y,x-y\rangle
\quad\hbox{for every }x\hbox{ in every cell incident to the minimal face of }y.
$$
In particular, the support extends over entire incident cells. The constants can be enlarged once so that both conclusions use the same pair $A_X,B_X$.

The metric conclusion is cellwise, and consequently bounds variation along any finite polygonal path whose segments lie in cells by its Euclidean length. It is not an unqualified ambient-distance statement across nonincident cells or components. For example, two disjoint parallel affine lines, each carrying a positive balanced one-dimensional weight, can have different affine slopes. The ambient distance between corresponding points stays fixed while their function values separate linearly. Their union meets the main hypotheses with $C=0$.

**Theorem 2 (working296, all five units).** Let $\sigma$ be a nonempty closed rational convex cell in its rational affine hull $Q$. Let $\ell$ be an actual real affine function on $Q$ whose slope is strictly positive on every nonzero direction in $\rec(\sigma)$. Suppose $f$ is finite continuous convex on $\sigma$, $|f-\ell|\leq C$, and $f$ has a finite global Euclidean Lipschitz constant. There is a proper convex real piecewise-affine auxiliary function $\Gamma$ on all of $Q$, with rational spatial carrier, equal to $\ell$ on all of $\sigma$. There is a finite continuous convex function $F$ on all of $Q$, equal to $f$ on $\sigma$, with $|F-\Gamma|\leq C$. For every $\eta>0$ and every prescribed finite set of rational points of $\sigma$, there is a genuine finite convex real piecewise-affine majorant $P$ on $Q$, with rational spatial carrier, such that $F\leq P\leq F+\eta$, with equality at the prescribed points and with $P^\infty=\Gamma^\infty$. Restriction gives uniform above-approximants on $\sigma$ with the actual cell recession. A common dyadic shift gives uniformly decreasing approximants. Exact contacts refer to the unshifted construction.

When $f$ is as in Theorem 1 and $\ell=\gamma|_\sigma$ for an admitted positive-growth real PA PC reference, the Lipschitz assumption in Theorem 2 is supplied by Theorem 1. The auxiliary $\Gamma$ does not replace the actual reference on $X$.

**Theorem 3 (working297, all three units).** On the unbalanced orthant $\sigma=\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$, let
$$
\gamma(x,y)=x+y,
\qquad f(x,y)=x+y+\max(0,1-\sqrt{xy}).
$$
This is continuous convex, differs from $\gamma$ by a number in $[0,1]$, and has the same recession. Every finite continuous real PA function $a$ on this orthant satisfies $\|a-f\|_\infty\geq\tfrac12$. The bound is attained by $a=\gamma+\tfrac12$. This is a boundary diagnostic outside the balanced domain, not a counterexample to Theorem 1 or to the original balanced task.

# Elementary foundations used in the reconstruction

We disclose the following ordinary foundations: completeness of the real numbers; compactness of closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space; elementary Gaussian elimination and finite-dimensional linear algebra; the product rule and divergence theorem on polyhedral domains with spherical truncation; and one-variable convex secant inequalities. Here are the additional consequences we need, with proofs to specify their scope.

**Finite cones and a coefficient bound.** For a fixed finite list $v_1,\ldots,v_m$, every vector in their nonnegative cone has a representation using a linearly independent sublist. Indeed, if positive coefficients have dependent columns, take a nonzero dependence $\sum_i b_i v_i=0$, reversing its sign to have a positive entry. Subtract $s b_i$ from the coefficients, where $s=\min_{b_i>0} a_i/b_i$. Coefficients remain nonnegative, a positive coefficient becomes zero, and the represented vector does not change. Repeat. For each independent sublist $I$, its column map has a linear inverse on its image. Thus
$$ \sum_{i\in I} a_i\leq K_I\|v\|. $$
There are only finitely many sublists; their maximum $K$ works for every vector in the cone. This also proves that the cone is closed: for a convergent sequence of represented vectors choose a subsequence with one independent sublist; its coefficients are bounded and converge along a further subsequence. The empty cone is $\{0\}$ and has coefficient bound zero.

If a point $w$ is outside a closed convex cone $K$, nearest-point separation is elementary. A nearest point $k\in K$ exists by restricting the distance minimization to a sufficiently large closed ball. First variation gives $\langle w-k,z-k\rangle\leq0$ for $z\in K$. Scaling $k$ and using $0\in K$ gives $\langle w-k,k\rangle=0$. Consequently $v=w-k$ satisfies $\langle v,z\rangle\leq0$ on $K$ and $\langle v,w\rangle=\|v\|^2>0$. This is the only cone separation needed below.

**Finite polyhedral generators and projections.** A rational cone given by finitely many homogeneous inequalities has a rational basis for its lineality space, obtained from the joint kernel of its rows. Split off this space using a rational complementary subspace. In the pointed quotient, orient the rows as nonnegative functions on the cone. Their sum is positive on every nonzero vector; otherwise all rows vanish, giving lineality. Its section at value one is bounded: an unbounded sequence, normalized and passed to a unit limit, would give a nonzero cone vector at value zero. A bounded polyhedron is the convex hull of finitely many vertices. To see this without importing a representation theorem, at a nonvertex point choose a nonzero direction annihilating its active rows. Moving in both signs reaches additional active rows, since the polyhedron is bounded. The original point is a convex combination of the two endpoints. Induction on active-row rank ends at vertices. Vertices solve finitely many independent systems. Rational systems have rational solutions. This proves finite rational generation of the pointed cone; adjoin both signs of a rational lineality basis.

Homogenizing a nonempty polyhedron $A x\leq b$ as $A t\leq\alpha b$, $\alpha\geq0$, gives, by the same cone result,
$$ P=\conv\{s_1,\ldots,s_r\}+\cone\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}. $$
Generators with positive $\alpha$ yield the $s_i$; those with zero $\alpha$ yield recession directions. All spatial data are rational when the original rows are rational. Conversely, a finite convex hull plus a finite cone is a polyhedron: express it using nonnegative coefficients, a sum-one equality for hull coefficients, and a linear image. Eliminate variables one at a time. For one variable, pair every lower bound with every upper bound and retain rows not involving that variable. These finite weak inequalities are exactly the condition that the interval of allowable values is nonempty; if one side is absent the interval is unbounded and still nonempty. Equalities are two inequalities. This proves finite elimination, over either real or rational coefficients, and rationality of the projected polyhedron when the spatial data are rational. These arguments also apply in a relative affine hull.

**Local convex bounds and relative subgradients.** A finite convex function $u$ on a relatively open neighborhood of $q$ has local Lipschitz bounds, hence continuity, and a relative subgradient at $q$. Choose a closed cube centered at $q$ inside that neighborhood. Convexity bounds $u$ above by the largest vertex value. Reflection about $q$ gives a lower bound on a smaller cube. On a still smaller cube, extend the segment between any two points a fixed positive distance in either direction within the bounded cube; the convex secant inequalities bound its slope by the oscillation divided by that distance. This proves local Lipschitzness without presupposing continuity.

For existence of a subgradient, use the closed convex epigraph over this cube. Project $(q,u(q)-t)$ to it, and normalize the vector from the projection to that point. As $t\downarrow0$ the projections converge to $(q,u(q))$; compactness of the unit sphere supplies a limiting nonzero supporting normal. Its vertical component is nonpositive because the epigraph contains upward rays. It cannot be zero: a nonzero purely spatial functional cannot have its maximum over a spatial neighborhood at its center. Dividing by the negative vertical component gives an affine lower support. Convex secants extend this local support over the entire original convex domain. A zero-dimensional relative domain has the zero subgradient. The same argument on full affine space proves that a finite continuous convex function is the supremum of all its affine supports. In particular its double convex conjugate equals itself. No general duality theorem is being imported here.

# L0: real endpoint PCC and convexity on inherited closed cells

Fix incident cells $\sigma_i\succeq\tau$ and a real PCC configuration with $\alpha_i>0$; delete zero coefficients first. Write perspective variables
$$ (\alpha_i,t_i),\qquad t_i=\alpha_i x_i. $$
The conditions $x_i\in\sigma_i$, $\sum\alpha_i=1$, and $\sum t_i\in\tau$ are finitely many rational weak linear inequalities and equalities in these variables. For example, $A_i x_i\leq b_i$ becomes $A_i t_i\leq\alpha_i b_i$. Equations for relative affine hulls are included. Add $\alpha_i\geq0$.

At the given configuration, impose as equations every inequality that is active. This is its minimal feasible face. Gaussian elimination gives a rational particular solution and a rational basis for the homogeneous solution space. Rational combinations are dense in that affine space. All inactive rows have strictly positive slack at the given point, and there are only finitely many; sufficiently close approximations preserve these inequalities. They also preserve $\alpha_i>0$. Thus the given configuration is approximated by rational feasible configurations. Their endpoints $t_i/\alpha_i$ and centers $\sum_i t_i$ are rational, and their coefficients are permitted printed PCC coefficients. A center in the relative interior stays there under sufficiently close feasible approximations; for a boundary center use its minimal inherited face, which is contained in every assigned incident cell. Apply printed PC there and take limits using continuity of $f$. This proves PCC for real endpoints, real centers, and real coefficients in every fixed face incidence.

For two real points in one inherited closed cell $\sigma$, their convex combination belongs to a unique minimal face $\tau\preceq\sigma$. Assign both endpoints to $\sigma$, and apply the just-proved real PCC at that center. This proves convexity of $f$ on $\sigma$. No face is merged or coarsened. In particular, convexity on an inherited closed face follows without any automatic-continuity assertion about raw rational-point PC functions.

# L1: quantitative distance and uniform insets

Let $P=\{x:n_j\cdot x\leq b_j\}$ be nonempty in a fixed Euclidean affine hull, with equality constraints already removed by working in that hull. A nearest point $z$ to $x$ exists by compactness in a sufficiently large ball. Put $w=x-z$, and let $J$ be the active rows at $z$. We claim
$$ w\in\cone\{n_j:j\in J\}. $$
Otherwise cone separation proved above gives $v$ with $n_j\cdot v\leq0$ for all active rows and $w\cdot v>0$. For sufficiently small $s>0$, $z+s v$ satisfies the inactive rows, by their positive slack, and also every active row. Nearest-point first variation would require $w\cdot v\leq0$, a contradiction.

Independent-column elimination gives $w=\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j n_j$ with $\lambda_j\geq0$ and $\sum\lambda_j\leq H\|w\|$, where $H$ depends only on the finite row list, not on the right-hand sides or active subset. Hence, for $\delta(x)=\max(0,\max_j(n_j\cdot x-b_j))$,
$$
\|w\|^2=\sum_j\lambda_j(n_j\cdot x-b_j)
\leq H\delta(x)\|w\|,
\qquad \dist(x,P)\leq H\delta(x).
$$
Zero rows cause no difficulty; a nonempty system has their right-hand sides nonnegative, and they never help a nonzero representation. An empty row list gives the whole affine hull and distance zero. In dimension zero the assertion is also immediate. This is a proof of the needed distance estimate, including its uniformity; the name of a distance theorem is not a substitute for the argument.

For a face $\tau$, list all its own facet inequalities, together with all inequalities of every incident top cell whose restrictions have strictly positive slack on $\ri(\tau)$. Constraints identically equal on $\tau$ are not strengthened. A valid affine inequality on $\tau$ which vanishes at one relative interior point vanishes everywhere on $\tau$; otherwise its affine restriction would change sign in a small relative neighborhood. This explains the dichotomy and the finite list.

Choose a rational point $z_0\in\ri(\tau)$, and a rational margin $\delta_\tau>0$ below every listed slack at $z_0$. Strengthen every listed row by that margin, retaining the other defining constraints of $\tau$. The resulting inset $\tau^\delta$ is nonempty. For every $y\in\tau$, the violation of each strengthened row is at most $\delta_\tau$. The preceding distance estimate gives a nearest point $z\in\tau^\delta$ with
$$ \|z-y\|\leq D_\tau:=H_\tau\delta_\tau. $$
This estimate holds uniformly near lower faces and at infinity. A fixed interior anchor alone would give no such uniform bound. If the list is empty, take $\tau^\delta=\tau$ and $D_\tau=0$. A zero-dimensional face also has $z=y$ and $D_\tau=0$, even when some listed restrictions are positive constants.

For any finite list of assigned tangent-cone generators $v_j$, choose one rational $\varepsilon_\tau>0$ sufficiently small that
$$ z+\varepsilon_\tau v_j\in\sigma(j)
\quad\hbox{for every }z\in\tau^\delta.
$$
Indeed, an incident-cell row active on $\tau$ is respected by the assigned cone direction. Every other row has slack at least $\delta_\tau$ on the inset, and its possible positive change is bounded by $\varepsilon_\tau\max_j|n\cdot v_j|$. Affine-hull equalities are preserved. Finiteness supplies one choice for all rows and generators. Empty-list and zero-dimensional cases are included by the same reasoning.

# L2: positive real balancing fills the local span

At $y\in\ri(\tau)$ the tangent cones $C_{\sigma,\tau}$ of incident top cells are independent of the choice of $y$: they are given by the rows active identically on $\tau$, with lineality containing $T_\tau$. They are rational polyhedral cones of dimension $d$. By the elementary generation result, choose finite rational generators for them, including both signs of a rational basis of $T_\tau$, each assigned to an incident top cell. Put
$$ E_\tau=\Span\bigcup_{\sigma\succeq\tau} C_{\sigma,\tau}. $$

The star inherits balancing. A facet of a tangent cone comes from a facet of its cell containing $\tau$, the adjacent star cells are exactly the adjacent original cells there, and their tangent lattices and quotient primitive normals are unchanged. A rational refinement preserves balancing as well: a new facet in the interior of an old cell has two opposite primitive quotient directions with equal inherited weight; an old facet is subdivided with its old relation unchanged. This specifies rather than assumes the local inheritance used here.

For a facet $\rho\prec\sigma$, write $c_\sigma=\covol(N_\sigma)$ and $c_\rho=\covol(N_\rho)$ in their Euclidean spans. Saturation implies $N_\sigma/N_\rho$ is free of rank one. A lattice basis for $N_\rho$, together with a lift $u$ of its primitive quotient generator, is a basis for $N_\sigma$. The parallelepiped volume identity therefore gives
$$ \|u_\perp\|=c_\sigma/c_\rho,
\qquad u_\perp=(c_\sigma/c_\rho)\nu_{\sigma/\rho}, $$
where $\nu_{\sigma/\rho}$ is the inward Euclidean unit conormal. Consequently actual real balancing is exactly the stationary unit-conormal flux relation
$$
\sum_{\sigma\succ\rho}\rho_\sigma\nu_{\sigma/\rho}=0,
\qquad \rho_\sigma=w_\sigma c_\sigma>0.
$$
This covolume conversion is essential: replacing primitive normals by unit normals without it is generally incorrect.

Let $K$ be the conical hull of the finite generators in $E_\tau$. It is closed. Suppose $K\ne E_\tau$. The cone separation argument supplies a nonzero linear functional $\lambda$ on $E_\tau$ that is nonnegative on $K$. It is positive somewhere on the union of the cones, since that union spans $E_\tau$.

Apply the divergence theorem on each $C_{\sigma,\tau}\cap B(0,1)$ to the constant vector obtained by projecting $\nabla\lambda$ to $T_\sigma$, with density $\rho_\sigma$. Its divergence is zero. The sum of planar facet fluxes cancels by the preceding stationary relation, with outward conormals the negatives of the displayed inward conormals. The remaining spherical flux is
$$
\sum_\sigma \rho_\sigma
\int_{C_{\sigma,\tau}\cap S^{d-1}_{T_\sigma}}\lambda(\theta)\,dS(\theta).
$$
Every term is nonnegative. One is strictly positive: if $\lambda$ is positive on a point of a full-dimensional cone, it is positive on a relatively open spherical patch of that cone. Lower-dimensional edges have zero boundary measure. This contradicts zero total flux.

In dimension one the same argument is the two-endpoint divergence formula on intervals or rays, with counting measure on the unit sphere. A whole line has canceling antipodal endpoints. Cones with lineality are handled by the same ball truncation; no pointedness assumption is needed. If $T_\tau=E_\tau$, its two-sided tangent basis already proves the conclusion. In dimension zero, $E_\tau=\{0\}$. These observations cover zero relative codimension and the degenerate cases without a complete-plane hypothesis.

We have proved $K=E_\tau$. Independent-column elimination now gives one finite geometric constant $K_\tau$ such that both $v$ and $-v$ admit assigned nonnegative generator representations with coefficient sums at most $K_\tau\|v\|$. The constant is calculated from finitely many inverse column maps. Actual weight magnitudes do not enter that bound; their positivity and balancing were needed to prove that the cone fills the span.

# L3: finite directional costs and supports on whole incident cells

Assume $f|_\tau$ has global Lipschitz constant $M_\tau$. For a point face set $M_\tau=0$. Fix $y\in\ri(\tau)$ and choose the inset point $z$ of L1. Write $\xi=z-y$, so $\xi\in T_\tau$ and $\|\xi\|\leq D_\tau$. For a feasible direction $w\in C_{\sigma,\tau}$, define
$$ h_\sigma(w)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(y+t w)-f(y)}t. $$
Convex secants show that this limit exists in $[-\infty,\infty)$: a fixed feasible positive secant bounds it above, but initially it may equal $-\infty$. Positive homogeneity follows by a change of variable. Midpoint convexity, applied to $y+2t u$ and $y+2t v$, shows
$$ h_\sigma(u+v)\leq h_\sigma(u)+h_\sigma(v). $$
This extended-real inequality is legitimate before finiteness: no term can be $+\infty$, and if one right-hand term tends to $-\infty$, the midpoint bound forces the corresponding upper limit to be $-\infty$. Tangent directions have common derivatives in all incident cells, since a small segment in either tangent direction stays in $\tau$. In particular $h_\sigma(-\xi)\leq M_\tau D_\tau$ and is finite.

For an assigned generator $v_j$, L1 puts $y+\xi+\varepsilon v_j=z+\varepsilon v_j$ in its cell $\sigma(j)$. The bound to the *same* affine restriction of $\gamma$ gives
$$ h_{\sigma(j)}(\xi+\varepsilon v_j)
\leq 2C+G(D_\tau+\varepsilon\|v_j\|). $$
Subadditivity applied to $\varepsilon v_j=(\xi+\varepsilon v_j)+(-\xi)$ gives the uniform generator upper bound
$$
h_{\sigma(j)}(v_j)\leq U_\tau,
\qquad U_\tau=\frac{2C+(G+M_\tau)D_\tau}{\varepsilon_\tau}+G V_\tau,
\quad V_\tau=\max_j\|v_j\|.
$$
An upper bound here allows a value $-\infty$; we remove that possibility next, instead of assuming it away.

Any finite list of assigned feasible directions $w_a$ with $\sum_a w_a=0$ has feasible endpoints $y+t w_a$ for one common sufficiently small $t>0$. Their equal-weight barycenter is $y$. The real-endpoint PCC of L0 gives
$$ \sum_a\frac{f(y+t w_a)-f(y)}t\geq0. $$
If an incident derivative $h_\sigma(w)$ were $-\infty$, append a fixed-generator representation of $-w$ from L2, using its nonnegative coefficients as scalings of the assigned directions and deleting zeros. Every appended directional quotient has a finite upper limit, bounded by its coefficient times $U_\tau$. The sum would tend to $-\infty$, contradicting the displayed PCC. Thus every incident directional derivative is finite. Taking limits now shows that every finite zero-sum assigned list has nonnegative total derivative cost.

Define, over *all* finite assigned incident-direction decompositions,
$$
H_y(v)=\inf\left\{\sum_a h_{\sigma(a)}(w_a):
w_a\in C_{\sigma(a),\tau},\ \sum_a w_a=v\right\}.
$$
The empty decomposition has cost zero at $v=0$. The generator representation gives $H_y(v)\leq K_\tau U_\tau\|v\|$. Append a generator representation of $-v$ to any candidate decomposition of $v$; the zero-sum cost inequality gives the opposite bound. Consequently
$$ -K_\tau U_\tau\|v\|\leq H_y(v)\leq K_\tau U_\tau\|v\|. $$
There is no $-\infty$ infimum. Scaling decompositions proves positive homogeneity for positive scalars; the zero-sum property proves $H_y(0)=0$. Concatenating two decompositions whose costs are within a positive tolerance of their finite infima proves subadditivity. These properties and the two-sided bound imply that $H_y$ is globally Lipschitz with constant $K_\tau U_\tau$.

Apply the full-space epigraph-support construction from the foundations to this finite continuous sublinear function at zero. It gives a linear functional $p_y\leq H_y$. Testing both $v$ and $-v$ gives $\|p_y\|\leq K_\tau U_\tau$. Extend it by zero on $E_\tau^\perp$ to an ambient vector. For every $x$ in an incident cell, $x-y\in C_{\sigma,\tau}$ and convex secants give
$$
f(x)-f(y)\geq h_\sigma(x-y)\geq H_y(x-y)\geq\langle p_y,x-y\rangle.
$$
The support therefore holds on the entire closed incident cell, including its far end and its boundary, rather than only on a germ. When $E_\tau=\{0\}$ take $p_y=0$, omitting all generator maxima and inverse constants. A zero-dimensional face in a positive-dimensional complex still has a nonzero local span in general and uses the full construction. All uses of real PCC, extended-real limits, subadditivity, and supports have now been justified.

# L4 and L5: induction over every face and the quantitative conclusion

Order all the finitely many faces by dimension. Before handling a face $\tau$, supports have been constructed at all points of its proper faces, by using each point's minimal face. Let $B$ be the maximum of their norm bounds, or zero if there are no proper faces. These supports hold on all of $\tau$: any top cell containing $\tau$ is incident to the minimal face of each such boundary point.

At $q\in\ri(\tau)$, relative subgradients exist by the foundations. Let $a$ be *any* such subgradient. If $a\ne0$, put $e=a/\|a\|$ and consider $q+t e$. Because $q$ is relatively interior, it is feasible for a positive initial interval. If the ray exits at a finite $t_0$, its endpoint $z$ belongs to a proper face. The subgradient at $q$ and the already constructed support at $z$ imply
$$
t_0\|a\|\leq f(z)-f(q)\leq t_0\langle p_z,e\rangle\leq t_0 B.
$$
If it never exits, bounded difference from the affine restriction gives
$$
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(q+t e)-f(q)}t=\langle a_\gamma,e\rangle\leq G,
$$
while the subgradient inequality bounds every such secant below by $\|a\|$. Thus every relative subgradient has norm at most $M_\tau=\max(B,G)$. The zero subgradient already satisfies this bound. For a zero-dimensional face use the sharper $M_\tau=0$.

Supports at two relative interior points give the Lipschitz inequality there. To pass to arbitrary points of the closed face, mix each point with a fixed relative interior point using the same positive mixing parameter, then let that parameter decrease to zero and use continuity. This proves *global* Lipschitzness on the whole possibly unbounded face. L3 now supplies its uniform ambient support bound
$$ B_\tau=K_\tau\left(\frac{2C+(G+M_\tau)D_\tau}{\varepsilon_\tau}+G V_\tau\right). $$

This is induction over all finite faces, not a vertex-started induction. A minimal positive-dimensional face has no proper faces; every relevant ray then remains forever, so the recession argument starts the induction. Lineality presents no problem. An affine top cell with no proper faces is also included. Positivity of $f$, positive growth of $\gamma$, averaging of references, independence of quotient normals, and a complete-plane assumption are absent from the argument.

For explicit dependence, suppose proper-face support bounds have coefficients $A_\rho C+B_\rho G$. Set
$$ a_\tau=\max_{\rho\prec\tau} A_\rho,\quad
b_\tau=1+\max_{\rho\prec\tau}B_\rho, $$
with empty maxima zero. Then $M_\tau\leq a_\tau C+b_\tau G$. One admissible next support coefficient pair is
$$
A_\tau=K_\tau\left(2/\varepsilon_\tau+a_\tau D_\tau/\varepsilon_\tau\right),
\quad B_\tau^{\rm coeff}=K_\tau\left((1+b_\tau)D_\tau/\varepsilon_\tau+V_\tau\right).
$$
Zero-dimensional faces have Lipschitz bound zero but may have nonzero ambient support bounds obtained from L3 when the ambient local span is nonzero. Thus one must not set their ambient support bound to zero unless the entire local span is zero. This distinction is retained in the recursion. Taking maxima of the finitely many Lipschitz and support coefficient pairs proves Theorem 1. Summing the cellwise inequality on the segments of an admissible polygonal path proves its stated intrinsic consequence. This completes L0--L5 of working299; the regularization input supplied by L5 is a cellwise input and not a gluing theorem.

# C1 and C2: a rational-wall auxiliary reference on one affine hull

Identify the rational affine hull $Q$ with a Euclidean affine space and write
$$ \sigma=\{x\in Q:A_j\cdot x\leq b_j\},\qquad
\ell(x)=a\cdot x+b. $$
All constraint rows are rational; the slope $a$ and constant $b$ are actual reals. Put
$$ \delta(x)=\max(0,\max_j(A_j\cdot x-b_j)),\qquad
\Gamma(x)=\ell(x)+\kappa\delta(x), $$
where $\kappa$ is a positive integer to be chosen. The violation function is convex PA with rational walls. Adding the same real affine function to all its pieces leaves those walls rational. Thus $\Gamma$ is a genuine scalar real PA function, exactly equal to $\ell$ on the entire cell.

Let $r(v)=\max(0,\max_j A_j\cdot v)$. The recession function of $\Gamma$ is
$$ h(v)=a\cdot v+\kappa r(v). $$
On the compact set $S=\rec(\sigma)\cap\{\|v\|=1\}$, the assumed slope has a positive minimum if $S$ is nonempty. It remains positive in a neighborhood of $S$ on the unit sphere. On the compact complement of a smaller such neighborhood, $r$ has a positive minimum; a sufficiently large integer $\kappa$ makes $h$ positive there as well. If $S$ is empty, $r$ is positive everywhere on the unit sphere and the same conclusion follows directly. Hence $h(v)\geq c\|v\|$ for some $c>0$. Since $\Gamma-h$ is uniformly bounded by the finitely many constant terms in its affine pieces, $\Gamma(x)\geq c\|x\|-D$ after choosing an origin. This proves proper coercive growth. The zero-dimensional case is a constant on a point and is proper, with the recession condition vacuous. A full positive-dimensional affine space cannot satisfy the slope assumption on both $v$ and $-v$, so there is no overlooked full-space example contradicting that assumption.

The L1 distance proof applies verbatim to this cell, with a finite constant $H$ and $\dist(x,\sigma)\leq H\delta(x)$. This independently verifies C1. The preceding construction verifies C2. It is an auxiliary extension only; neither its values off $\sigma$ nor its coefficients are substituted for the actual reference on other cells.

# C3: an exact finite convex extension, with no intermediate operator

Choose a rational number $M$ at least the global Lipschitz constant of $f$ on $\sigma$. Define on all of $Q$
$$ \widehat f(x)=\inf_{y\in\sigma}\{f(y)+M\|x-y\|\}. $$
It is finite: a fixed $y_0\in\sigma$ gives an upper bound, and Lipschitzness and the triangle inequality give the lower bound $f(y_0)-M\|x-y_0\|$. For $x\in\sigma$, every summand is at least $f(x)$ and the choice $y=x$ gives equality. The triangle inequality inside the infimum proves global $M$-Lipschitzness. Convexity follows by taking approximate minimizers at two points, using their convex combination in $\sigma$, the convexity of $f$, and the triangle inequality for the norm, and then letting the approximation tolerance go to zero. Attainment of the infimum is unnecessary and is not asserted.

For a nearest point $y\in\sigma$,
$$
\widehat f(x)\leq f(y)+M\|x-y\|
\leq\ell(x)+C+(M+\|a\|)\dist(x,\sigma)
\leq\Gamma(x)+C
$$
provided the integer $\kappa$ is also at least $H(M+\|a\|)$. Increasing $\kappa$ preserves C2. Set
$$ F(x)=\max\{\widehat f(x),\Gamma(x)-C\}. $$
Then $F$ is finite continuous convex on all of $Q$, $\Gamma-C\leq F\leq\Gamma+C$, and $F=f$ on the entire $\sigma$. The last equality uses $\Gamma|_\sigma=\ell$ and $f\geq\ell-C$. This maximum is a maximum of continuous convex functions, with no piecewise-affine claim about $\widehat f$ or $F$. No Monge--Ampere measure or mixed operator is applied to this intermediate function. This completes C3.

# C4: full-affine primal majorants, including real heights and boundary fibers

We reconstruct the full-affine mechanism rather than citing a grant label. Let $Q$ have positive dimension; the point case is immediate. A finite convex real PA function $\Gamma$ on $Q$ is the maximum of its finitely many actual affine pieces. Each full-dimensional piece is a global affine support by convex secants; lower-dimensional pieces are their continuous traces. Thus
$$ \Gamma(x)=\max_j(a_j\cdot x+b_j),\qquad
h(v)=\Gamma^\infty(v)=\max_j a_j\cdot v. $$
Let $D=\conv\{a_j\}$. This compact polytope need not be rational. The coercive inequality $h(v)>0$ for nonzero $v$ implies that zero is in its interior. If zero is outside $D$, its nearest point gives a direction with $h(v)<0$ by first variation. If zero lies on its boundary, take outside points tending to zero, normalize their nearest-point separating normals, and pass to a unit limit; first variation then gives $h(v)\leq0$ for that nonzero limit. Both cases contradict positivity. Both $\Gamma-h$ and $F-h$ are bounded on all of $Q$.

Define the actual conjugate $F^*(p)=\sup_x(p\cdot x-F(x))$. Its finite domain is exactly $D$. For $p\in D$, $p\cdot x\leq h(x)$ bounds the supremum uniformly above, while evaluation at a fixed $x$ bounds it below. For $p\notin D$, let $q$ be its nearest point in $D$ and $v=p-q$. First variation gives $\max_{z\in D}v\cdot z\leq v\cdot q<v\cdot p$, so $p\cdot v>h(v)$ and $x=t v$ makes the supremum infinite. On $D$ the conjugate is convex, lower semicontinuous, finite, and bounded: convexity and lower semicontinuity follow directly from being a supremum of continuous affine functions.

The needed continuity includes boundary fibers. More generally a finite lower semicontinuous convex function $g$ on a compact polytope is continuous relative to that polytope. It is bounded above by the largest value at its finitely many vertices. At $p$, choose $r>0$ below every inactive facet slack divided by the corresponding row norm. If $q$ is near $p$ in the polytope, the point $z=p+r(q-p)/\|q-p\|$ stays in it: active rows do not increase, and inactive rows have the chosen margin. Convexity gives
$$ g(q)\leq g(p)+(\|q-p\|/r)(B-g(p)). $$
Together with lower semicontinuity this proves continuity at every boundary point as well as in the interior. Work in the relative affine hull for lower-dimensional polytopes; the single-point case is immediate. This proof does not assume rational facets of $D$.

By continuity of $F$, rational spatial samples compute the same supremum defining $F^*$. For each $p\in D$, choose a rational $s$ whose value $p\cdot s-F(s)$ is within $\eta/2$ of $F^*(p)$. Continuity of the latter on $D$ and of the displayed affine function makes the error less than $\eta$ on a neighborhood of $p$. Compactness supplies a finite set of rational samples $A$ such that
$$ F^*(p)-\eta\leq g_A(p):=\max_{s\in A}(p\cdot s-F(s))\leq F^*(p)
\quad(p\in D). $$
Append any prescribed finite rational contact set. Enlarging $A$ preserves both inequalities. The sample heights remain the *actual real numbers* $F(s)$; they are not rounded.

The recession epigraph has finitely many exact rays with rational spatial projections. Indeed the rational recession cones of the finite carrier of $\Gamma$ cover $Q$: along a ray a subsequence lies in one carrier cell, and its defining inequalities show that the direction lies in that cell's recession cone. On each such cone $h$ is linear. Take the finite sign chambers of all their defining homogeneous rational row hyperplanes together with rational coordinate hyperplanes. They give a common finite rational refinement, and its coordinate orthants make its cones pointed. Use their rational generators $r_k$. Then
$$ \epi h=\cone\{(r_k,h(r_k)),(0,1)\}. $$
For a direction in one cone, a nonnegative generator representation gives exactly its height because $h$ is linear there; the vertical ray accounts for any additional height. The spatial generators are rational, but their heights may be irrational. This is the exact recession cone, not a rationalized slope surrogate.

Form the primal polyhedron
$$ E=\conv\{(s,F(s)):s\in A\}+\epi h. $$
It is closed: the first set is compact, the cone is closed, and a convergent sum sequence has a convergent compact summand and hence a convergent cone summand. It is a finite real polyhedron by the elementary elimination argument. Its spatial projection is all of $Q$, since the projection of $\epi h$ is all of $Q$; every fiber contains an upward ray.

Convex secants and bounded $F-h$ show $F(x+v)\leq F(x)+h(v)$: compare the unit secant along $v$ with arbitrarily long secants and pass to infinity. Convex combinations of the sample lifts followed by adding a point of $\epi h$ therefore remain in $\epi F$. Thus $E\subseteq\epi F$. Every fiber has a finite attained bottom, defining a finite convex function $P$ with $E=\epi P$. It is continuous by the local convex bound proof, since its domain is the full affine space.

Direct optimization over the hull coefficients and cone gives
$$ P^*(p)=g_A(p)\quad(p\in D),\qquad P^*(p)=+\infty\quad(p\notin D). $$
For $p\in D$ the supremum over the cone is zero; outside $D$ it is infinite along a separating recession ray. The double-conjugate identity proved from full-space supports in the foundations now gives
$$ F\leq P\leq F+\eta\quad\hbox{on all of }Q. $$
At every retained sample, the lift belongs to $E$, so $P(s)\leq F(s)$; the lower inequality gives equality. This proves finite-contact exactness and a global uniform error, not merely convergence on a bounded set.

We must check rational walls despite irrational heights. Every lower graph face of $E$ is exposed by a functional with negative vertical coefficient. Full spatial projection rules out vertical facets, and any graph face is the intersection of lower facets, so a positive sum of their exposing normals has negative vertical coefficient. Its exposed hull summands are a subset of the sample points, and its exposed cone summands are a subset of the exact rays with zero exposing value. The vertical ray is not among them. On the graph face, projection is an affine isomorphism, since that face lies on one affine graph. Its projected cell is consequently
$$ \conv\{\hbox{rational sample locations}\}+\cone\{\hbox{rational spatial rays}\}, $$
a rational polyhedron by the elementary projection proof. Intersections project to common faces: the graph over a common projected point is unique, and the affine graph projection on each face preserves its face lattice. The finite projected lower-face complex covers $Q$. On it $P$ is real affine and continuous.

Finally this is the genuine scalar-extension notion of real PA, rather than a collection of arbitrary irrational-wall formulas. The coefficient tuples for continuous affine functions on this rational carrier satisfy rational matching equations, obtained by testing equality on rational affine bases of shared faces. Their solution space has a rational basis by Gaussian elimination. Clear denominators in each basis tuple to make its slopes integral on the fixed lattice and its constants rational. Every actual real coefficient tuple is a real linear combination of these rational PA basis functions. Thus $P$ belongs to the required scalar real PA space. The same argument applies to $\Gamma$. No generic closure of real PA under an arbitrary maximum with irrational switching walls has been assumed.

The recession of $E$ is exactly $\epi h$. Inclusion of this cone is immediate. For the reverse inclusion, divide a recession sequence by its parameter; the bounded hull part disappears and closedness leaves its direction in the cone. Equivalently use the homogenized finite representation. Hence $P^\infty=h$. Ordinary full-space Jensen convexity directly implies every printed PCC for restrictions at feasible barycenters. It also gives local nonnegative divisor inequalities on any positive balanced test cycle: subtract a supporting affine function which agrees with the cell's tangent gradient, then each incident inward residual slope is nonnegative and the balanced affine contribution vanishes. This justifies the PC property without importing a converse criterion and does not manufacture a mixed measure on an unbalanced cell.

An exact one-dimensional illustration retains an irrational height. Take $F(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}$ and reference $\Gamma(x)=|x|$. The second derivative of $F$ is $(1+x^2)^{-3/2}>0$, and $0<F-\Gamma\leq1$. The two samples at $x=\pm1$ have actual height $\sqrt2$. Their primal hull plus $\epi|v|$ gives
$$ P(x)=\sqrt2+\max(0,|x|-1). $$
Its spatial walls are exactly the rational points $-1,1$, its sample contacts are exact, and its recession is $|v|$. For $r=|x|\leq1$, $P^2-F^2=1-r^2\geq0$; for $r\geq1$, $P^2-F^2=2(\sqrt2-1)(r-1)\geq0$. Both functions are positive. Also $P-(\sqrt2-1)$ equals $1$ in the first region and $r$ in the second, each at most $F$. Thus $0\leq P-F\leq\sqrt2-1$ globally, with equality at zero. The exact finite program checks these comparisons in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ on its specified rational inputs; the displayed inequalities prove the whole-line assertion. Restrict the rational carrier of $P$ to $\sigma$ by intersection. The resulting rational carrier is finite, the restriction is convex real PA, and
$$ f\leq P|_\sigma\leq f+\eta. $$
Prescribed rational contacts are exact because $F=f$ on $\sigma$. On $\rec(\sigma)$, $r(v)=0$, so $h(v)=a\cdot v$, the actual recession of $\ell$. Bounded $f-\ell$ has that same recession along every feasible ray. This verifies the actual same cell recession without altering the reference. C4 is complete.

Choose $\eta_n=2^{-n}$ and unshifted majorants $p_n=P_n|_\sigma$ with $0\leq p_n-f\leq\eta_n$. They may all preserve the same prescribed finite rational contact set. Define
$$ g_n=p_n+4\eta_n. $$
Then $4\eta_n\leq g_n-f\leq5\eta_n$, while
$$ g_n-g_{n+1}\geq4\eta_n-5\eta_{n+1}=\tfrac32\eta_n>0. $$
Thus $g_n$ decreases uniformly to $f$ on the whole cell, remains real PA on a rational carrier, and has the same recession. The shifted functions do not retain exact contacts; the unshifted ones do. The maximum interval error of a chord is its interval length squared divided by four. This example proves the logical insufficiency of finite contact constraints for entire-face trace matching. Nor do separate convex supports on different incident cells ensure a single ambient vector satisfying all their support inequalities. The simultaneous direction-cost argument of L3 applies to the original printed-PC function; it has not been proved for arbitrarily chosen independent PA approximants.

# B1--B3: the unbalanced orthant boundary diagnostic

On the positive open quadrant, the Hessian quadratic form of $\sqrt{xy}$ is
$$ -\frac{(y\,dx-x\,dy)^2}{4(xy)^{3/2}}. $$
Thus the geometric mean is concave there. Continuity and inward approximation extend its concavity to the closed orthant. Alternatively, the concavity inequality follows directly by squaring and the two-term Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. Hence $1-\sqrt{xy}$ is convex and continuous on the closed orthant, and so is its maximum with zero. Adding $x+y$ proves continuity and convexity of $f$. Its difference from $\gamma$ lies in $[0,1]$. The slope of $\gamma$ is strictly positive on every nonzero orthant recession direction. Dividing the bounded difference by the ray parameter shows $f^\infty(v)=v_1+v_2$. These are the full B1 assertions.

Every continuous finite real PA function on a convex cell is globally Lipschitz with the maximum of the norms of its finitely many intrinsic gradients. For any segment, each carrier cell cuts it in a closed interval, possibly empty or a point. The finitely many interval endpoints partition the segment into finitely many subsegments on which one affine formula applies. Sum the affine Lipschitz bounds over these subsegments, using continuity at their endpoints. This argument allows actual real coefficients and even real walls; rational walls are not needed for the diagnostic. Apply it also to $a-\gamma$, obtaining some finite constant $L$.

Let $z_n=(n^2,0)$ and $w_n=(n^2,n^{-2})$. Their Euclidean distance is $n^{-2}$, while $(f-\gamma)(z_n)=1$ and $(f-\gamma)(w_n)=0$. If $e=\|a-f\|_\infty$ is finite, the triangle inequality gives
$$ 1\leq2e+L n^{-2}. $$
Letting $n\to\infty$ proves $e\geq1/2$. If $e$ is infinite the assertion is immediate. The real PA function $a=\gamma+1/2$ attains exactly $1/2$, so the floor is sharp. This verifies all of B2 on the continuum; bounded exact computations in the accompanying program illustrate the limiting inequality but do not replace it.

The same pair has $f(z_n)-f(w_n)=1-n^{-2}$ at distance $n^{-2}$, so $f$ is not uniformly continuous and is not globally Lipschitz on the orthant. At a boundary point $(x,0)$ with $x>0$, the inward $y$ directional quotient equals $1-\sqrt{x}/\sqrt t$ for small $t$ and tends to $-\infty$. A finite convex extension to an open neighborhood would be locally Lipschitz by the foundational cube argument and cannot have this derivative. This explains why the Lipschitz input to C3 cannot be deleted.

A single positive weighted orthant is unbalanced along either axis: there is only one inward primitive normal and no opposite contribution. Its boundary star lies in a proper halfspace. The positive-flux contradiction of L2 therefore does not apply. This verifies B3 and precisely locates the diagnostic outside the main theorem. It supplies no original balanced counterexample and has no mixed-operator interpretation in this paper.
